extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, fiction writers, and students of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and judging novels, covering story vs. plot, character construction, pattern, style, rhythm, truth, and other craft concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs. Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'story' (a narrative of events: 'There was once…') from 'plot' (a sequence of events linked by causation). Plot imposes cause-and-effect relations on events; story can be simply a report of happenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work simply recounts events or shapes them causally; consider whether causation is needed for satisfaction. Avoid mistaking a mere series of incidents for a plotted novel; conversely, don't force artificial causation where story suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as Causal Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong plot gives events a causal backbone—one thing leads to another because of motives, obstacles, and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for believable motives and causal links rather than coincidences. Plotters arrange incidents so the reader can see why each event follows; avoid implausible leaps or gratuitous twists that lack justification in character or circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: People (Authentic Characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's aim should be to present 'people'—characters who seem alive and individual—rather than mere abstractions or theatrical types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters behave as if they have inner lives and histories. Characters should resist being reduced to single traits; the writer should reveal habits, contradictions, and specific details that make them feel real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are constructed around a single idea or quality and are simple enough to be summed up in a sentence; they are useful for carrying themes or recurring functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters are not necessarily failures: they can be effective when the work needs recognizable, repeatable figures (e.g., comic or symbolic roles). Avoid letting every character be flat; they work best as supporting elements or in genres that require archetypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters are complex, capable of surprising the reader in convincing ways; their behaviour cannot be fully anticipated from a brief summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether surprising actions feel motivated by the character's whole personality. Roundness requires nuance and change; a truly round character has inner contradictions and development across the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Surprise vs. Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may surprise us, but the surprise must be believable—consistent with the deeper truth of the character rather than arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good surprise is one that, in hindsight, feels inevitable because it grows out of underlying traits. Avoid surprises that betray established character without plausible development or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Types and Symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Types and symbolic figures can be employed for structural or thematic purposes, but they risk flattening human complexity if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use types when the pattern or message requires them, but balance them with individualizing detail so they don't become mere puppets or slogans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern and Unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel should achieve an artistic pattern—a meaningful arrangement of incidents, motifs, and echoes that produce a whole greater than the sum of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repetitions, contrasts, and arrangements that create coherence and resonance. Pattern may be formally strict or subtle, but it should yield a sense of design rather than randomness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy and Imaginative Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy (in the sense of imaginative invention, images, and symbols) is a legitimate element of the novel and can illuminate truth when handled with control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether imaginative or fantastical touches deepen understanding of character or theme rather than simply decorating the narrative. Avoid fantasy that distracts from the human reality at the book's core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy (Sense of Universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond reporting events, a novel may attain prophetic quality—revealing truths about human nature or society that feel generally applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the novel's insights transcend its particulars without lapsing into abstract moralizing. Prophecy should come from careful depiction, not preachy statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth to Human Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's obligation is to present truth—psychological and moral plausibility—even when inventing details; truth in fiction means fidelity to human motives and reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge scenes and reactions for psychological believability. Even improbable plots can be successful if the human responses within them ring true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and Tempo
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel must have rhythm—an ebb and flow in pacing, sentence length, incident density, and emotional intensity that gives the reader a sense of movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author controls speed appropriately: accelerating in moments of crisis, pausing for reflection when needed. Poor rhythm manifests as monotony, rushed climax, or overlong digression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Style should be appropriate to the novel's subject and tone: clear, exact, and musical when required; avoid meaningless ornament or forced cleverness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concrete detail, apt metaphors, and a voice that serves the story. Beware of purple prose, excessive abstraction, or stylistic tricks that call attention away from the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration and Point of View
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of narrative voice and point of view is essential; the choice (omniscient, limited, first person, etc.) must be maintained or altered with clear purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate consistency and appropriateness: does the chosen viewpoint allow necessary knowledge without authorial intrusions that break illusion? Sudden, unexplained shifts of perspective weaken authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling vs. Showing (Narrative Modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both 'telling' (summary, commentary) and 'showing' (scenes dramatized in detail) are tools; neither is inherently bad, but each must be used where it best serves the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize either excess: endless telling flattens experience; endless showing can become tedious. Use telling for necessary compression or reflection and showing for moments of change or revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should suggest life rather than slavishly reproduce speech; it must reveal character and advance the story while remaining intelligible and purposeful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge dialogue by how much it reveals indirectly—social position, education, temperament—without becoming mere exposition. Avoid transcript-like realism that burdens the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour and Irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour and irony are valuable devices for adding layers of meaning and for controlling tone, but they must match the novel's moral seriousness and pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether comedic elements undercut or enrich the central concerns. Irony should illuminate contradictions rather than simply mock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Coincidence and Chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidences and chance events are permissible when they contribute to pattern or theme, but overreliance on chance to solve plot problems is weak artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow coincidences that fit the novel's logic or symbolic design; condemn deus ex machina solutions that rescue characters without psychological or causal groundwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending and Sense of Completion
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel's ending should produce a satisfying artistic closure—either resolving central tensions or leaving intentional, thematically grounded open questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the ending follows organically from the work's pattern and character development; avoid abrupt reversals or sentimental wrap-ups that betray earlier truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and Selective Omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Good novels exercise economy: they include what matters and omit extraneous material, trusting readers to infer rather than over-explaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise judicious omission that sharpens focus; fault over-description, irrelevant episodes, or didactic passages that interrupt the narrative flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial Attitude and Moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's moral stance should be implicit in depiction rather than delivered as overt moralizing or sermonizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for subtlety—showing consequences and letting readers reach judgments. Heavy-handed ethical commentary weakens imaginative engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural Control (Arrangement of Parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond individual scenes and sentences, the novelist must arrange episodes, motifs, and characters architecturally to produce an integrated work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the placement of episodes, repetition of motifs, and balancing of subplots. Disordered arrangement produces reader confusion; careful architecture yields emergent meaning.
